title: Lesson 4: Group Problem-Solving Exercise
summary: Problems should not become opportunities for blame or gossip. Practise the SOLVE method so the team identifies facts, agrees on action and reviews the result together.

items.label: Duration
items.body: 60–90 minutes

items.label: Participants
items.body: All Zura Spa staff

items.label: Method
items.body: Group discussions, case studies, role-playing, decision-making and practical assessments

sections.title: 1. Introduction: Problems are easier to solve when people work together
paragraphs: Imagine it is a busy Saturday at Zura Spa.

A client arrives for a confirmed appointment. The receptionist discovers that the booking was recorded for the wrong time. The therapist who was supposed to attend to the client is already occupied. The client becomes upset.

The receptionist blames another employee. The therapist complains that reception is always disorganised. Another employee begins discussing the incident with colleagues. Meanwhile, the client is still waiting. Several people are talking, but nobody is solving the problem.
Now imagine a different approach.

The receptionist acknowledges the booking problem and informs the supervisor. The supervisor checks the available options. The therapist communicates her actual availability. Another employee helps with an appropriate operational task. The client receives an accurate explanation and is offered an authorised solution. Afterward, the team reviews how the booking error occurred and how to prevent it.
The problem may not disappear immediately, but the employees are now working toward a solution.
The difference between these two situations is not the absence of problems. It is the team's ability to solve them together.

At Zura Spa, problems should not become opportunities for blame, gossip or unnecessary conflict. They should become opportunities to demonstrate communication, accountability, cooperation and sound judgment.

sections.title: 2. What is group problem-solving?
paragraphs: Group problem-solving is the process of bringing people together to understand a challenge, consider possible solutions, agree on appropriate action and evaluate the outcome.
It requires employees to contribute their knowledge, experience and observations toward a shared goal.
Group problem-solving is not a competition to prove who is smartest or who is right. It is a cooperative effort to identify the most appropriate solution.
list: Identifying the actual problem.
Establishing relevant facts.
Listening to different perspectives.
Understanding how the problem affects others.
Considering possible solutions.
Agreeing on responsibilities.
Taking appropriate action.
Reviewing the result.
Preventing recurrence where possible.

sections.title: 3. Why group problem-solving matters at Zura Spa
paragraphs: Different employees understand different parts of daily operations.

Receptionists understand booking arrangements and client enquiries. Therapists understand treatment-room preparation and the practical requirements of their services. Supervisors coordinate responsibilities, resolve operational conflicts and make decisions within their authority.
When relevant information is brought together, the team can often understand a problem more accurately.
A team becomes stronger when employees learn how to solve problems together instead of creating additional problems through their reactions.
list: It encourages employees to listen to one another.
It reduces unnecessary assumptions.
It helps identify the actual cause of problems.
It improves coordination between departments and roles.
It develops confidence in decision-making.
It strengthens accountability.
It encourages practical solutions rather than complaints.
It helps prevent repeated mistakes.

sections.title: 4. The difference between complaining and problem-solving
paragraphs: Complaints can sometimes identify genuine concerns.
However, an effective employee should try to explain the concern clearly and contribute to an appropriate solution.
Identifying a problem is useful. Understanding it and helping resolve it is even more valuable.
table: "Who is responsible, and what support is needed?"
"Which part of the process needs improvement?"
"What specific action should be considered by management?"

sections.title: 5. Rules for today's group exercises
paragraphs: Before beginning, the trainer should explain the following rules.
The trainer should remind participants that the scenarios are hypothetical learning exercises.
The purpose is to practise professional responses, not to investigate or publicly judge individual employees.
list: Listen without interrupting.
Respect every participant's contribution.
Focus on the problem, not personalities.
Do not use exercises to embarrass real colleagues.
Avoid gossip, insults and unnecessary accusations.
Ask questions when information is unclear.
Consider client safety, privacy and professional standards.
Do not assume authority to approve refunds, prices or unfamiliar treatments.
Allow quieter participants to contribute.
Agree on practical actions and clear responsibilities.

sections.title: 6. The SOLVE method
paragraphs: For today's exercises, every group should use the SOLVE method.

Example: An appointment was recorded incorrectly. State that a confirmed appointment was entered for the wrong time. Observe by checking the booking record and the client's confirmation. List available appointment alternatives and appropriate client communication. Verify that the authorised employee confirms a workable solution. Evaluate how the error occurred and whether the booking confirmation process needs improvement.
This method helps the team avoid reacting emotionally before understanding the situation.

items.label: S — State the problem
items.body: Describe what happened without exaggeration or personal attacks.

items.label: O — Observe and establish the facts
items.body: Identify what is known, what remains unclear and who has relevant information.

items.label: L — List possible solutions
items.body: Consider safe, realistic options and their likely consequences.

items.label: V — Verify and implement the best action
items.body: Confirm authority, assign responsibilities and carry out the agreed response.

items.label: E — Evaluate and prevent recurrence
items.body: Review the result and identify improvements for future situations.

sections.title: 7. How to organise the exercise
paragraphs: The trainer should divide participants into groups of three to five, depending on attendance.
For smaller groups, one participant may perform more than one role.
The trainer can adjust the timing to suit the number of participants.

items.label: Facilitator
items.body: Ensures everyone contributes.

items.label: Recorder
items.body: Writes down the group's decisions.

items.label: Presenter
items.body: Explains the proposed solution.

items.label: Timekeeper
items.body: Helps the group stay within the allocated time.

sections.title: 8. Group exercise 1: The double booking
paragraphs: Duration: 7 minutes.

Two clients have been booked for the same therapist at 4:00 p.m. Both clients have received confirmations. The therapist cannot attend to both clients simultaneously. One client has already arrived. The receptionist discovers the error and becomes anxious. The therapist is frustrated because the mistake affects her schedule.
The trainer reveals facilitator guidance after the group discussion.
list: What is the immediate problem?
What facts must be confirmed?
What should the receptionist do first?
How should the therapist respond?
What options should the supervisor consider?
How should the affected client be informed?
What can prevent similar errors?

sections.title: 9. Group exercise 2: The incomplete treatment room
paragraphs: Duration: 7 minutes.

A therapist finishes a session but leaves the treatment room without completing the required reset. Another therapist has a client arriving shortly. She enters the room and discovers that used linen has not been removed and fresh supplies are missing. She becomes angry and wants to confront her colleague immediately.
The trainer reveals facilitator guidance after the group discussion.
list: What should be prioritised?
How should the room be made ready safely?
Should the therapists argue while the client waits?
How should the incomplete reset be reported?
How can responsibilities be clarified?
What should happen if this becomes a repeated problem?

sections.title: 10. Group exercise 3: The struggling new employee
paragraphs: Duration: 7 minutes.

A newly employed receptionist is learning the appointment system. She makes several mistakes during her first week. An experienced employee becomes frustrated and says: "I don't understand why you keep making mistakes. This work is not difficult." The new receptionist becomes embarrassed and stops asking questions. Her errors continue.
The trainer reveals facilitator guidance after the group discussion.
list: What is the main problem?
How has the experienced employee contributed to the situation?
What responsibility belongs to the new receptionist?
What training support is needed?
How can the supervisor evaluate progress?
How can corrections be communicated respectfully?

sections.title: 11. Group exercise 4: The missing payment
paragraphs: Duration: 7 minutes.

A receptionist reviews the day's payment records and discovers that one completed session does not have a corresponding verified payment entry. She is unsure whether the client paid through another approved channel or whether the payment was omitted. Another employee suggests: "Just mark it as paid. We can sort it out later."
The trainer reveals facilitator guidance after the group discussion.
list: What facts should be verified?
Why is marking an unverified payment as paid inappropriate?
Who should be informed?
What records should be checked?
How should the discrepancy be documented?
How can similar issues be prevented?

sections.title: 12. Group exercise 5: The angry client
paragraphs: Duration: 7 minutes.

A client complains that her appointment began late. She is visibly upset and raises her voice at reception. The receptionist feels attacked and begins responding defensively. A therapist overhears the conversation and wants to intervene.
The trainer reveals facilitator guidance after the group discussion.
list: How should the receptionist respond?
What information should be established?
Should the therapist intervene, and under what circumstances?
When should a supervisor become involved?
What solutions may be considered within company policy?
How can the team avoid making the situation worse?

sections.title: 13. Group exercise 6: The disagreement between colleagues
paragraphs: Duration: 7 minutes.

Two therapists disagree about responsibility for arranging supplies. One believes the task belongs to the employee who completed the previous session. The other believes it belongs to the employee preparing for the next appointment. Their disagreement becomes personal. They stop communicating with each other.
The trainer reveals facilitator guidance after the group discussion.
list: What is the actual issue?
What information is needed to resolve it?
Why are personal attacks unhelpful?
How should the supervisor clarify responsibility?
How should both employees behave afterward?
What can prevent similar disputes?

sections.title: 14. Group exercise 7: The busy Saturday challenge
paragraphs: This is the main team simulation.
It is 3:00 p.m. on Saturday. Zura Spa has several appointments scheduled close together.
Each group must develop a coordinated response. The solution must identify immediate priorities, individual responsibilities, necessary communication and any required supervisory decisions.
The trainer reveals the model solution after the group discussion.
list: Two clients arrive at nearly the same time.
One treatment room is not ready.
A therapist reports that fresh towels are running low.
A client requests an appointment change.
A new employee is unsure about her assigned responsibility.
Reception is handling multiple enquiries.
One therapist has finished a session and is available for a short period.

items.body: Which problem should be addressed first?
What can be handled simultaneously?
What should reception do?
What should the therapists do?
What should the available employee do?
How should the new employee be supported?
Which decisions require supervisory approval?
What should be communicated to clients?
What standards must not be compromised?
What should be reviewed after the busy period?

sections.title: 15. Group decision-making challenge
paragraphs: Not every suggested solution is appropriate. Some solutions may be quick but unsafe. Others may be convenient but dishonest. An excellent team should consider the consequences before acting.
Complete the five decision questions in the Lesson 4 Knowledge Check at the bottom of this lesson.
list: A client is waiting, but the treatment room has not completed its required cleaning. Allow the client in immediately to avoid delay / Complete the required cleaning and communicate any necessary delay / Ask the client to ignore the room condition
A payment discrepancy is discovered. Record only verified information and report the discrepancy / Assume payment was received / Delete the incomplete record
Two employees disagree about a task assignment. Stop communicating with each other / Discuss the disagreement with unrelated colleagues / Check the assigned procedure and seek clarification
A new employee is struggling with a task. Mock the employee / Provide appropriate guidance and supervised practice / Complete every task for the employee indefinitely
An employee is overwhelmed during a busy shift. Request appropriate assistance and clarify priorities / Hide the workload problem / Respond rudely to colleagues

sections.title: 16. Role-play: From conflict to cooperation
paragraphs: Activity duration: 10–15 minutes. The trainer should select three participants.

Round 1 — Poor teamwork: The receptionist becomes defensive. The therapist responds angrily. Both employees blame one another. The client is left waiting. No practical solution is agreed upon. The trainer stops the role-play after a short period.

Round 2 — Professional teamwork: The receptionist acknowledges the error. The therapist communicates the operational impact respectfully. The supervisor establishes the facts. The team considers available solutions. Responsibilities are assigned. The client receives appropriate communication.
Expected outcome: Participants recognise that respectful communication and accountability make problem-solving more effective.

items.label: Employee A
items.body: A receptionist who has made a booking error.

items.label: Employee B
items.body: A therapist affected by the error.

items.label: Employee C
items.body: A supervisor coordinating the response.

list: Which approach resolved the problem more effectively?
What changed between the two rounds?
Which training lessons were demonstrated?
How can employees apply the same approach during real operations?

sections.title: 17. How to evaluate group performance
paragraphs: The trainer can score each group using the following guide.
26–30: Excellent teamwork and problem-solving.
21–25: Good performance with minor areas for improvement.
16–20: Developing skills; further practice recommended.
15 or below: Significant improvement needed.
The score should support learning, not become a competition that embarrasses participants.

sections.title: 18. Common mistakes to avoid during group problem-solving
paragraphs: A solution is only effective when it is appropriate, implemented and reviewed.

items.label: 1. Jumping to conclusions
items.body: Employees assume they know the cause before checking the facts.

items.label: 2. Blaming people immediately
items.body: The discussion becomes about personalities rather than responsibilities.

items.label: 3. Ignoring quieter employees
items.body: Important information may be missed because only outspoken participants contribute.

items.label: 4. Choosing the fastest solution without considering safety
items.body: A quick decision may create a more serious problem.

items.label: 5. Failing to assign responsibility
items.body: The group agrees that something should be done, but nobody is responsible for doing it.

items.label: 6. Making unauthorised commitments
items.body: Employees promise refunds, appointment changes or services without the necessary approval.

items.label: 7. Failing to follow up
items.body: The immediate problem is addressed, but the underlying cause remains.

sections.title: 19. Personal reflection: What kind of problem-solver am I?
paragraphs: Employees should consider their usual response when problems occur.
Rate each statement: 1 = Rarely, 2 = Sometimes, 3 = Usually, 4 = Consistently.
Maximum score: 40. This is a reflection exercise, not a formal performance appraisal.
table: I try to understand the facts before drawing conclusions.
I listen to colleagues even when I disagree.
I avoid blaming people without evidence.
I contribute practical solutions rather than only complaints.
I accept responsibility for my own mistakes.
I ask for help or supervisory guidance when necessary.
I consider client safety and professional standards.
I support agreed solutions even when my suggestion was not selected.
I reflect on what can prevent similar problems.

sections.title: 20. Personal assignment
paragraphs: Each employee should answer the following questions in writing.
list: Explain what group problem-solving means.
Identify five benefits of group problem-solving at Zura Spa.
Describe the difference between complaining and problem-solving.
Explain the SOLVE method.
Why is it important to establish facts before making decisions?
How can employees disagree respectfully during problem-solving?
What should a team do when an appointment is double-booked?
How should employees respond when a colleague makes a mistake?
Why should quieter employees be encouraged to contribute during group discussions?
Explain why a quick solution is not always the best solution.
Describe how responsibilities should be assigned after a decision is made.
Identify one recurring workplace challenge and propose a practical way to address it without naming or embarrassing individual colleagues.

sections.title: 21. Seven-day problem-solving challenge
table: Identify a minor operational problem and describe it factually
Practise listening to another person's perspective
Ask a clarifying question before making an assumption
Suggest a practical improvement through the appropriate channel
Follow up on a responsibility assigned to you
Reflect on what worked and what could improve

sections.title: 22. Final lesson and takeaway
paragraphs: Group problem-solving is an essential part of building a strong Zura Spa team.
Problems will arise. Appointments may change. Employees may make mistakes. Supplies may run low. Clients may become dissatisfied. Colleagues may disagree.
The presence of these challenges does not automatically mean a team is unsuccessful. What matters is how employees respond.
An effective team identifies problems early, communicates respectfully, establishes facts, considers appropriate solutions and takes responsibility for agreed actions.
Employees should not allow ego, gossip, fear or personal rivalry to prevent cooperation.
They should remember that the goal is not to prove who is right but to achieve the best responsible outcome for clients, colleagues and the organisation.
Next topic: Personal Commitment to Teamwork and Professional Growth.

remember: At Zura Spa, problems should bring our minds together, not drive our relationships apart. When something goes wrong, do not rush to accuse someone or defend yourself before understanding the facts. Listen carefully, communicate respectfully and focus on what needs to be done. A strong team is not one where everybody always agrees or where mistakes never occur. It is one where employees can face challenges together, accept responsibility, contribute ideas and work toward practical solutions. The ability to solve problems professionally is one of the clearest signs that teamwork has moved beyond words and become part of our workplace culture.
